skills.name: Drama: plot, conflict and stage evidence

note.text: Drama presents action for performance through dialogue and stage directions. Plot is the organised development of action; conflict is a clash of aims, obligations or forces that drives choices. Conflict can occur within a character as well as between people. Stage directions can shape movement, pauses and audience knowledge. A character’s spoken claim is not automatically a fact endorsed by the playwright.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain a dramatic conflict using dialogue, stage directions and changing action. Builds on: prose characterisation and creative scenes. Leads to: narrative reconstruction and later drama analysis.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original scene: [At a locked hall. Bih holds a notice; Tabe carries chairs.] Bih: The notice says our group booked this room. Tabe: The organiser gave us the same time. [They compare the notices.] Bih: Let us ask before moving anything. The competing bookings create the conflict. Comparing notices changes the action from assertion towards checking evidence. No prescribed play is being replaced by this invented scene.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify each aim and the obstacle. Cite dialogue or a stage direction, then explain how it moves the action. Distinguish an assertion, an observed action and a possible performance choice.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: dialogue: words spoken by dramatic characters.
stage direction: written guidance for action or presentation in performance.
conflict: a clash of aims or pressures motivating action.
plot development: an organised change in action or situation.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: Bih says the notice gives her group a booking.
They compare the notices directs an observable action.
The groups appear to have competing room bookings.
Comparing the notices moves the scene towards verification.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Everything a character says is proved true by being spoken. Correction: Speech can express a claim, misunderstanding or intention.
Stage directions must always be spoken aloud by characters. Correction: They guide performance rather than necessarily belonging to dialogue.
Conflict must always involve physical violence. Correction: Competing aims can drive a non-violent dramatic conflict.
Plot is only a list of unrelated character names. Correction: Action develops through connected events and choices.

pick.q: Original scene: [Ngozi hides a damaged cup.] Ngozi: Nothing happened. What should a reader distinguish?
pick.r: The spoken denial from the action supplied by the stage direction
w: The denial as proof no cup exists
A stage direction that must be shouted
e: The direction explicitly mentions a damaged cup.
A character’s denial is not the author’s belief.
Directions guide performance, not automatic speech.
pick.y: The audience can know something different from the spoken claim.

pick.q: Original scene: Ayuk wants to disclose a mistake but fears losing the club’s trust. What conflict is shown?
pick.r: An internal conflict between competing pressures
w: No conflict because only one person is named
e: No battle is described.
A character can experience internal conflict.
No court or ruling is stated.
pick.y: Drama can develop an inward dilemma.

pick.q: Original scene: [Bih reads the notice again, then hands it to Tabe.] How can this direction affect the scene?
pick.r: It stages a pause and a shared look at evidence
w: It proves every booking issue is resolved
It removes the need for any actor
It makes the notice’s contents automatically false
e: Checking is not a final resolution.
The action still requires performance.
Reading and sharing do not establish falsity.
pick.y: Explain the action’s effect without inventing an outcome.
